edits.name: Explicit restricted isometries beyond the square-root barrier (Tao's deterministic UUP question)
edits.field: Compressed sensing; frame theory; incidence geometry
edits.statement: A restricted isometry quantifies how well a measurement matrix preserves the Euclidean geometry of sparse vectors in compressed sensing. For an $m \times n$ matrix $\Phi$, the restricted isometry constant $\delta_k$ is the smallest $\delta$ with $(1-\delta)\|z\|_2^2 \le \|\Phi z\|_2^2 \le (1+\delta)\|z\|_2^2$ whenever $|\operatorname{supp}(z)| \le k$. Random matrices give $\delta_k \to 0$ with $m/n \to 0$ and $k = m^{1-o(1)}$. In 2007 Tao asked for deterministic constructions of comparable strength. Coherence arguments stop at $k \approx m^{1/2}$, and the best unconditional explicit constructions before this work (Bourgain, Dilworth, Ford, Konyagin and Kutzarova, 2011, and later refinements) reached $k = m^{1/2+\varepsilon_0-o(1)}$ with $\varepsilon_0$ at most about $8\cdot 10^{-8}$. What is the largest exponent $\alpha$ for which an explicit family has $m \to \infty$, $m/n \to 0$, $\delta_k \to 0$ and $k = m^{\alpha-o(1)}$, and can it reach the random exponent $\alpha = 1$?
edits.posedBy: Terence Tao, Open question: deterministic UUP matrices (blog post, 2 July 2007)
edits.model: GPT-6 Astra; ChatGPT (GPT-6 Pro); Claude Opus 5.5; GPT-6.1 Sol
edits.aiRole: Per the paper's disclosure, Theorem 1 was proved in one shot using GPT-6 Astra. While digesting the proof, the authors distilled the Gershgorin and flat-RIP hybrid estimate, identified the 2/3 barrier and explored subframes of two-distance tight frames, over several long conversations with ChatGPT. ChatGPT generated an initial draft; the authors then rewrote the paper completely and used ChatGPT and Claude Opus 5.5 for rounds of feedback. The authors state that they checked all mathematical claims, citations and computations and take full responsibility. The Lean formalization was created by a Claude Opus 5.5 orchestrator with GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra subagents.
edits.resultNote: Theorem 1: there is an explicit family of real $m \times n$ matrices with unit-norm columns such that $m \to \infty$, $m/n \to 0$, $\delta_k \to 0$ and $k = m^{2/3-o(1)}$. The unconditional exponent thus rises from barely above $1/2$ to $2/3$. The matrices are subframes of a two-distance tight frame built from the strongly regular graph $VO_4^-(p)$, $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$, with columns selected using Zahl's sphere-tangency bound over finite fields; the proof uses only the absolute values of the Gram entries, with no phase cancellation. Theorem 4 shows that $2/3$ is a barrier for every argument of that kind, and Proposition 10 shows that this construction itself cannot pass $2/3$. Exponents in $(2/3,1]$ remain open (Problem 9 of the paper), so Tao's question is answered only in part.

edits.name: Property $R_\infty$ for Artin groups (AIM Problem 8.6): the irreducible spherical case
edits.field: Geometric group theory; twisted conjugacy in Artin groups
edits.statement: A group $G$ has property $R_\infty$ if every automorphism $\varphi \in \operatorname{Aut}(G)$ has infinitely many twisted conjugacy classes, where $x$ and $y$ are $\varphi$-twisted conjugate if $y = z x \varphi(z)^{-1}$ for some $z \in G$. Problem 8.6 of the AIM problem list Geometry and topology of Artin groups asks: which Artin groups have property $R_\infty$? A remark by Ignat Soroko on the list records the property as known for the spherical types $A_n$ and $B_n$ ($n \ge 2$), $D_4$ and $I_2(m)$ ($m \ge 3$), for the Euclidean types $\tilde A_n$ and $\tilde C_n$ and for certain right-angled Artin groups, and as failing for abelian right-angled Artin groups.
edits.posedBy: AIM Problem List, Geometry and topology of Artin groups, Problem 8.6
edits.ageNote: The AIM list page with Problem 8.6 was archived on 13 February 2025; the year the problem was added was not confirmed here. Property R-infinity for Artin groups was studied earlier, for braid groups by Felshtyn and Goncalves (2010) and for other Artin groups by Juhasz (2010).

edits.resultNote: Theorem A: every irreducible Artin group of spherical type and rank at least two has property $R_\infty$. Types $A_n$, $B_n$, $D_4$, $I_2(m)$ (Calvez and Soroko) and $D_n$, $n \ge 6$ (Soroko and Vaskou) were known, and the paper notes that $D_5$ follows from a 2026 lemma of Paris and Soroko, so the new cases are $E_6$, $E_7$, $E_8$, $F_4$, $H_3$ and $H_4$. Proposition C: $A(I_2(5))/[P,P]$ has an automorphism with Reidemeister number 18, so the quotient does not inherit $R_\infty$. The proof relies on Cohen and Paris's computer-assisted theorem that $P$ is characteristic, which the authors did not re-run. Non-spherical Artin groups are not covered, so Problem 8.6 stays open in general.

edits.name: The Ideal Generation Conjecture for general points in projective space
edits.field: Commutative algebra; ideals of general points
edits.statement: Let $Z$ be a general set of $p$ distinct points in $\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ over an algebraically closed field $k$, with homogeneous vanishing ideal $I_Z \subset S = k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$, and let $D$ be the initial degree of $I_Z$. The Hilbert function of $S/I_Z$ is known, and $I_Z$ is generated in degrees $D$ and $D+1$. The Ideal Generation Conjecture (Geramita and Maroscia, 1984) predicts the number of minimal generators: the multiplication map $\mu_Z : (I_Z)_D \otimes_k S_1 \to (I_Z)_{D+1}$ has maximal rank, that is, it is injective or surjective. Before this work the conjecture was known in projective dimension at most four and for sufficiently many points. Does it hold for every number of points in every dimension?
edits.posedBy: A. V. Geramita and P. Maroscia (1984), as attributed by Gesmundo, Kayser and Telen (2025)
edits.ageNote: The manuscript cites Geramita-Orecchia (1982) and Geramita-Maroscia (1984) for the study of minimal generators; Gesmundo, Kayser and Telen call it a long standing conjecture and cite Geramita-Maroscia. It is the first step of Lorenzini's Minimal Resolution Conjecture, which is false in general.
edits.aiRole: The Hexagon provenance statement reads: this work was produced as a guided exploration by Open AI Astra agents. Hexagon labels the paper as primarily AI-generated text with human understanding of some parts; the PDF itself carries no AI statement. The Lean repository's provenance file names Vlado Vojdanovski as author and responsible maintainer and says OpenAI Codex agents (GPT-6) assisted with the Lean development, the exact finite certificates and the internal reviews; its metadata records the review status as agent-reviewed.
edits.resultNote: Theorem 1.1: let $k$ be algebraically closed of characteristic zero, $n \ge 2$, $D \ge 2$ and $N_j(n) = \binom{n+j-1}{j}$. For every $p$ with $N_{D-1}(n) \le p < N_D(n)$, a general reduced set $Z$ of $p$ points in $\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ has maximal-rank multiplication $(I_Z)_D \otimes_k S_1 \to (I_Z)_{D+1}$. So with $r = N_D(n) - p$ the ideal has $r$ minimal generators in degree $D$, $\max\{0,\ (n-1)(\tfrac{N_D(n)}{D+1} - r)\}$ in degree $D+1$, and none in higher degrees. The proof treats the statement as interpolation for $\Omega_{\mathbb{P}^{n-1}}(D+1)$ (vectorial Horace method), inducts on the degree for $D \ge 4$, and rests on explicit quadratic and cubic constructions with finite determinant calculations. Positive characteristic is not covered, and nothing is claimed about the higher syzygies of the Minimal Resolution Conjecture.
edits.verificationNote: No independent mathematician has checked this yet. Lean-checked on this site's ladder, not Lean-verified. Checked here on 19 November 2026: Hexagon page 2611.00274v1 with its provenance label, the paper's introduction and Theorem 1.1, and the conjecture as stated by Gesmundo, Kayser and Telen (arXiv 2307.02560, Conjecture 3). Challenge.lean (169 lines, Mathlib imports only) was read in full. For projective dimension $n \ge 1$, degree $d \ge 2$ and $\binom{n+d-1}{d-1} \le p < \binom{n+d}{d}$, it asserts a polynomial $\Delta$ on ordered affine-chart configurations, nonzero somewhere, such that wherever $\Delta \ne 0$ the points are distinct, the ideal is radical, the Hilbert function is $\min(N, p)$, the map $I_d \otimes S_1 \to I_{d+1}$ is injective or surjective, and the ideal has exactly the predicted minimal generators in degrees $d$ and $d+1$. That is Theorem 1.1 stated faithfully, with general meaning a nonempty Zariski open set. A grep of the 613 Lean files (about 172,000 lines) found no sorry outside the challenge stub and no axiom, native_decide, implemented_by, extern or unsafe. Not rebuilt here. The statement was written by the author's agents and is not independently anchored.
edits.significanceNote: A forty-year-old named conjecture on the minimal generators of the ideal of general points, the first step of the Minimal Resolution Conjecture, previously known only in projective dimension at most four and for many points; well known in commutative algebra and algebraic geometry, little known outside. edits.name: Quantum symmetry of circulant and abelian Cayley graphs beyond prime order
edits.shortName: Quantum symmetry of abelian Cayley graphs
edits.field: Quantum groups; quantum automorphism groups of graphs
edits.statement: For a finite graph $X$ with $N$ vertices let $G(X)$ be its automorphism group and $G^+(X) \subset S_N^+$ its quantum automorphism group, so that $G(X) \subset G^+(X)$; the graph has no quantum symmetry when this inclusion is an equality. Banica, Bichon and Chenevier proved that a circulant graph with a prime number $p$ of vertices and type $k$ has no quantum symmetry once $p > 6^{\varphi(k)}$, and wrote that they did not know what happens when the number of vertices is not prime, expecting some asymptotic result there as well. Which circulant graphs on a non-prime number of vertices, and more generally which Cayley graphs of finite abelian groups, have no quantum symmetry?
edits.posedBy: T. Banica, J. Bichon and G. Chenevier, Graphs having no quantum symmetry, Ann. Inst. Fourier 57 (2007)
edits.ageNote: The arXiv version of the posing paper is from May 2006 (math/0605257); the journal version appeared in 2007. According to the manuscript, Marashdeh raised the non-prime case again in 2026.
edits.aiRole: Claude Fable is listed as co-author on the paper's title page, and the Hexagon provenance statement reads: written by Claude Fable, with help from Teo Banica. Hexagon labels the text as primarily AI-generated, with human understanding of some parts. The source does not say which ideas came from the model and which from Banica, who is also one of the three authors of the 2007 paper that posed the question.
edits.resultNote: Theorem A: let $X$ be a Cayley graph of a finite abelian group $A$ of type $E \subset \operatorname{Aut}(A)$, with $|E| = k$ and every non-trivial element of $E$ having at most $m$ fixed points. If $|A| \ge k^2 m$ then $X$ has no quantum symmetry, and if $|A| \ge 2k^2 m$ then $G^+(X) = G(X) = A \rtimes E$. Theorem B: a circulant graph $\operatorname{Cay}(\mathbb{Z}_N, S)$ with $N = p^n$, $n \ge 2$, has quantum symmetry if and only if $S \cap \mathbb{Z}_N^*$ is a union of cosets of the subgroup of order $p$. Theorem C: a Cayley graph of type $E = \{\pm 1\}$ has quantum symmetry if and only if $A \cong \mathbb{Z}_4 \times \mathbb{Z}_2^n$. Open: circulant graphs of composite, non-prime-power order, where the paper conjectures (Conjecture 8.4, computer-checked by the authors for $N \le 43$) that quantum symmetry occurs exactly when $G(X)$ has two non-trivial automorphisms with disjoint supports; the dense prime case; graphs beyond abelian Cayley graphs.
edits.verificationNote: No independent mathematician has checked this yet. Checked here on 19 November 2026: the Hexagon page 2611.00305v1 with its provenance label, and the paper's introduction, Theorems A to D, Section 8 and Conjecture 8.4. The posed question was read in the introduction of Banica, Bichon and Chenevier (arXiv math/0605257), and the prime-order background in the abstract of Marashdeh's arXiv 2609.00462. As a sanity check, Theorem B was compared by hand with small cases that are known: the cycles $C_8$ and $C_9$ (no quantum symmetry) and $C_4$, $2K_2$, $3K_3$ and the complement of $3K_3$ (quantum symmetry); all agree. The proofs were not refereed here. The computer checks reported in the paper were not re-run, and no code link was found on the Hexagon record. No Lean formalization.

Published as Partial, Unreviewed, significance 8. Thank you.

The paper was read in its arXiv source on 19 November 2026. The AI statement in the acknowledgements (proofs generated with GPT-6, draft checked and rewritten with Claude Opus 5.5, under the authors' guidance) is quoted in the entry.

Edits, the mathematics untouched. Klee's 1969 question, whether every polygonal room is illuminable from every point, was answered by Tokarsky in 1995 without AI, so it cannot be the problem this entry records. edits.name: Tokarsky's question on the fewest sides of an unilluminable polygonal room, for lattice rooms
edits.field: Discrete geometry; polygonal billiards and illumination
edits.statement: A polygonal room has mirrored walls. A light ray reflects with equal angles and stops when it hits a corner. Two points $P$ and $Q$ of the room are mutually invisible if no light ray from $P$ reaches $Q$; a room containing such a pair is unilluminable. Tokarsky built the first polygonal example in 1995, with 26 sides, answering the illumination question published by Klee in 1969, and asked how few sides a polygon with two mutually invisible interior points can have. Rooms with 24 sides were found in 1996-97 and one of them was conjectured to be the smallest. All known examples are lattice rooms: unions of tiles of a reflection tiling in which every tile vertex outside a distinguished sublattice is a corner. This entry records the question inside that class: what is the least number of sides of a lattice room with one or with two invisible lattice points, and which rooms attain it?
edits.posedBy: George W. Tokarsky, Polygonal rooms not illuminable from every point, Amer. Math. Monthly 102 (1995), Example 3
edits.ageNote: The illumination question is attributed to Ernst Straus (early 1950s) and was first published by Klee in 1969; Tokarsky answered it in 1995 with a 26-sided room and asked for the fewest sides. Castro, Tokarsky and Thomson found 24-sided rooms in 1996-2001, and Stewart's 1997 Scientific American column records the conjecture that 24 is least. Tokarsky is a coauthor of the present paper.
edits.resultNote: Within lattice rooms only (arXiv:2611.13226, Table 1). A hole-free lattice room on the tiling by isosceles right triangles with one invisible lattice point (source) has at least 12 sides, attained only by the pinwheel; on the square tiling the least is 16. With two sources, hence two mutually invisible points, the least is 24 on the triangle tiling (exactly 12 rooms, plus 89 with 25 sides) and 34 on the square tiling (14 rooms). One post, one partition or one pinched hole lowers the two-source minimum to 18, 20 and 22; two and three posts give 17 and 16; a free hole gives 26. Three sources need at least 36 sides. A second class on the 30-60-90 tiling has minimum 27 (15 rooms). The classifications rest on exhaustive computer searches made finite by bounds proved in the paper. Still open, and stated as such by the authors: whether a simple polygon with fewer than 24 sides can have two mutually invisible interior points.

This work was done under the guidance of the authors from March 2026 onwards, and earlier versions of these models were used as well." The programs behind the exhaustive searches ship with the paper as ancillary files.

A small computation written here confirmed that the pinwheel as printed has 12 genuine corners, area 6, a single interior lattice point, and every other lattice point of the room at a corner. The authors' ancillary programs, whose saved log reports 19 of 19 checks passed, were not re-run here, and the reductions to finite searches were not refereed. edits.significanceNote: The illumination problem is famous as recreational mathematics, and the fewest-sides question has stood since 1995, but this result is a classification inside the special class of lattice rooms and leaves the general question open. Placed below Boshernitzan's conjecture for right and isosceles triangles (12), a named conjecture in polygonal billiards, level with the optimality of Ho's 1280-word code in the 19-dimensional kissing construction (8), which also closes one construction scheme by exhaustive search, and far below ergodicity of irrational triangle billiards (48).

edits.name: The supercritical Ten Martini Problem: Cantor spectrum for every analytic one-frequency Schrödinger operator with positive Lyapunov exponent
edits.field: Spectral theory; quasi-periodic Schrödinger operators
edits.statement: For a real analytic, nonconstant $v$ on $\mathbb{T}=\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$, an irrational frequency $\alpha$ and a phase $\theta$, consider the Schrödinger operator on $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z})$ $$(H_{v,\alpha,\theta}u)_n=u_{n+1}+u_{n-1}+v(\theta+n\alpha)u_n.$$ Its spectrum $\Sigma_{v,\alpha}$ does not depend on $\theta$. The Ten Martini Problem, posed for the almost Mathieu operator $v(x)=2\lambda\cos 2\pi x$ and solved by Avila and Jitomirskaya, asks that the spectrum be a Cantor set for every irrational $\alpha$. For general analytic $v$ this can fail where the Lyapunov exponent $L(E)$ vanishes (examples announced by Argentieri and Avila). The supercritical Ten Martini Problem is the conjecture that it never fails where $L(E)>0$: for every nonconstant analytic $v$ and every irrational $\alpha$, the part of the spectrum in the regime of positive Lyapunov exponent is a Cantor set.
edits.posedBy: Jiangong You, Sci. Sin. Math. 54 (2024), no. 6, 863-870, Conjecture 1; see also Marx and Jitomirskaya (2017)
edits.ageNote: The original Ten Martini Problem concerns the almost Mathieu operator and was solved by Avila and Jitomirskaya. The all-analytic supercritical form is cited by the paper to You's 2024 survey, Conjecture 1, and to Marx and Jitomirskaya 2017. You and Jitomirskaya are coauthors of the present paper. Before it, Cantor spectrum at all frequencies was known for Type I operators.
edits.resultNote: Theorem 1.1 of arXiv:2611.13068 (Ge, Jitomirskaya, You): for every nonconstant $v\in C^\omega(\mathbb{T},\mathbb{R})$ and every irrational $\alpha$, the set $\Sigma_{v,\alpha}\cap\overline{\mathcal O}$ is a Cantor set, where $\mathcal O=\{E: L(E)>0\}$. In particular the whole spectrum is Cantor whenever $L(E)>0$ throughout the spectrum, which by Sorets and Spencer holds for $\lambda v$ with $|\lambda|$ large. Nothing is claimed for subcritical energies, where intervals can occur. The paper notes the result cannot in general be strengthened to the dry version (all gaps open), citing a counterexample in preparation. The proof builds on two preprints by the same group, arXiv:2407.08866v3 (the intrinsic symplectic center) and arXiv:2609.15812 (The Robust Ten Martini Problem), both cited by the paper as arXiv preprints.

edits.name: The sharp lower bound for the canonical volume of threefolds of general type with positive geometric genus
edits.field: Algebraic geometry; explicit birational geometry of threefolds
edits.statement: For a complex projective threefold $X$ of general type with canonical singularities, the canonical volume is $$\operatorname{Vol}(X)=\limsup_{m\to\infty}\frac{6P_m(X)}{m^3},$$ which equals $K_Y^3$ on a minimal model $Y$ and can be a small rational number. J. A. Chen and M. Chen asked for the sharp lower bound of the volume among all threefolds of general type. For threefolds with geometric genus $p_g(X)>0$ the bound $1/30$ was proved by them when $\chi(\mathcal{O}_X)\le 0$, and it is attained by the hypersurface $X_{28}\subset\mathbb{P}(1,3,4,5,14)$; without that assumption the best general bound was $1/75$ (Chen-Chen 2015). What is the minimal canonical volume of a threefold of general type with $p_g>0$: is it $1/30$?
edits.posedBy: J. A. Chen and M. Chen (2008; Compos. Math. 2015, Open problem 1.1): find the sharp volume bound for threefolds of general type; here the case of positive geometric genus
edits.ageNote: Chen and Chen (J. Lond. Math. edits.name: Eremenko's conjecture: a bound linear in $n$ for the number of zeros of a polynomial $P(z,\bar z)$ of bidegree $(n,m)$
edits.field: Complex analysis; valence of harmonic and polyanalytic polynomials
edits.statement: A polyanalytic polynomial is a polynomial $P(z,\bar z)$ in a complex variable and its conjugate. Let $P$ have degree $n$ in $z$ and degree $m<n$ in $\bar z$, and suppose the equation $P(z,\bar z)=0$ has finitely many solutions. Bézout's theorem bounds their number by a quadratic expression in $n$ (Khavinson, Lundberg and Perry: $n^2+m^2$ under a coprimality assumption). For $m=1$ the sharp bound is $5n-5$ (Khavinson and Neumann), linear in $n$. Eremenko conjectured that this is general: for each $m\ge1$ there are constants $A_m$, $B_m$ such that the number of solutions is at most $A_m n+B_m$. Wilmshurst's more precise conjecture for harmonic polynomials, $3n-2+m(m-1)$, had been disproved in 2015.
edits.posedBy: A. Eremenko, The number of solutions of some non-holomorphic equations, unpublished note, 7 September 2026
edits.ageNote: Eremenko's note is dated 7 September 2026, two months before the solution. The paper traces the underlying problem of bounding the number of zeros to Sheil-Small (1992, 2002) and to Wilmshurst (1998) for harmonic polynomials, and says Khavinson, Lundberg and Perry formulated it for general polyanalytic polynomials (Problem 1.9 of their paper). Lundberg is a coauthor of the present paper.
edits.resultNote: Theorem 1.1 of arXiv:2611.13278 (Lundberg, Rosen, Zhang): if $n>m\ge1$, $f\in\mathbb{C}[z,w]$ has $\deg_z f=n$, $\deg_w f=m$ and $f(z,\bar z)$ has finitely many zeros, then their number is at most $(4m+1)n-5m$. So Eremenko's conjecture holds with $A_m=4m+1$, $B_m=-5m$; for $m=1$ this recovers $5n-5$. Proposition 4.1: for each fixed $m$ and all large $n$ there are examples with at least $(4m+1)(n-m)$ zeros, so the leading coefficient $4m+1$ is optimal. The exact maximum for $m\ge2$ stays open, and the examples are not harmonic, so the conjectured bound $2m(n-1)+n$ for harmonic polynomials (Lee, Lerario, Lundberg) is neither proved nor refuted. The proof builds a smooth surface of degree $n-m$ in $\mathbb{CP}^2$ whose genus is controlled by the number of zeros and applies the Kronheimer-Mrowka theorem (the Thom conjecture).

edits.name: Kim's dimension conjecture for the Chabauty-Kim method: projective curves over $\mathbb{Q}$
edits.field: Arithmetic geometry; rational points, Chabauty-Kim method
edits.statement: Let $X$ be a hyperbolic curve over $\mathbb{Q}$ with a rational basepoint, $p$ a prime, and $U_n^{\mathrm{et}}$, $U_n^{\mathrm{dR}}$ the level-$n$ quotients of its $\mathbb{Q}_p$-pro-unipotent etale and de Rham fundamental groups. Kim's Conjecture 1 says that for some $n$, possibly very large, $$\dim H^1_f(G_T,U_n^{\mathrm{et}})<\dim U_n^{\mathrm{dR}}/F^0,$$ where $H^1_f$ is the global Selmer variety. When the inequality holds, the integral points (the rational points, for projective $X$) lie in the zero set of a nonzero $p$-adic iterated integral, so they are finite and in principle computable. Kim derived the inequality from the Bloch-Kato or Fontaine-Mazur conjectures. Unconditionally it was known for the thrice-punctured line (Kim), for curves whose Jacobian is isogenous to a product of CM abelian varieties (Coates and Kim) and for solvable covers of $\mathbb{P}^1$ (Ellenberg and Hast). Does it hold for every smooth projective curve of genus $g\ge2$ over $\mathbb{Q}$?
edits.posedBy: Minhyong Kim, The unipotent Albanese map and Selmer varieties for curves, Conjecture 1 (arXiv 2005; Publ. RIMS 2009)
edits.ageNote: Conjecture 1 of Kim's paper, on arXiv as math/0510441 in October 2005 and published in Publ. RIMS in 2009. Known cases before this work: genus zero (Kim 2005), CM elliptic curves (Kim 2010), CM Jacobians (Coates-Kim 2010), solvable covers of the projective line (Ellenberg-Hast 2022).
edits.aiRole: From the paper's AI Declaration: the general strategy is the author's, or that of Coates and Kim, and the reduction from Galois cohomology to kernels of Iwasawa operators was done by the author about a year earlier. The nontrivial kernel bound (Theorem 3.1) and its application to the power-saving bound (Theorem 1.4) were developed in a long back-and-forth with GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI) in Ultra mode; the author then produced a dense 33-page draft to examine the argument with the model's help. Some ideas from those exchanges already appear in work of Weibo Fu (Annals 2024). The posted 61-page paper was written by the author without language models, apart from discussions of standard background and gathering references, and its proof of Theorem 3.1 is partly different and less technical than the preliminary one.
edits.resultNote: Corollary 1.5: for a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over $\mathbb{Q}$ of genus $g\ge2$ with a rational basepoint, and every odd prime $p$ of good reduction, the dimension inequality holds for all sufficiently large $n$, with no condition on the Jacobian's endomorphisms or Galois image. The key estimate (Theorem 1.4) is $$\dim H^2(G_{\mathbb{Q},\Sigma},L_n)<A\,\dim(L_n)\,n^{-1/(2g^2+g+1)},$$ with $L_n$ the degree-$n$ graded piece of the Lie algebra, deduced from a bound on $H^2$ of irreducible $\mathrm{GSp}_{2g}$-representations (Theorem 1.1). So the Chabauty-Kim loci are finite at large level, which reproves Faltings's theorem over $\mathbb{Q}$ by Kim's method. edits.name: The constant-width numerical range conjecture
edits.field: Matrix analysis; numerical ranges
edits.statement: The numerical range of a matrix $A\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times n}$ is $W(A)=\{x^*Ax: x\in\mathbb{C}^n,\ x^*x=1\}$, a compact convex subset of the plane. A convex set has constant width $d$ if its orthogonal projection onto every line has length $d$; disks have this property, and so do non-circular sets such as the Reuleaux triangle. Chien, Nakazato and Meng studied the diameter and width of numerical ranges, with constant-width examples among nilpotent Toeplitz matrices, and conjectured that a numerical range of constant width must be a disk. Is it true that the numerical range of every complex square matrix with constant width $d$ is a disk of radius $d/2$?
edits.posedBy: M.-T. Chien, H. Nakazato and J. Meng, The diameter and width of numerical ranges, Linear Algebra Appl. 582 (2019), 76-98
edits.ageNote: Conjectured by Chien, Nakazato and Meng (Linear Algebra Appl., 2019). Chien, Li and Nakazato (Linear Multilinear Algebra, 2021) extended the conjecture to higher-rank numerical ranges; that extension is not addressed by this proof.
edits.aiRole: From the paper's acknowledgements: the author used OpenAI's ChatGPT to explore proof strategies and to develop and refine the proof and its exposition, and takes responsibility for the mathematical arguments and the final manuscript. The model version is not stated. The same acknowledgements credit Ilya Spitkovsky with suggesting the use of characteristic roots separated by the width, which is the starting point of the argument, and Minwu Kim with checking an earlier version.
edits.resultNote: Theorem 1: for every $A\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times n}$, $n\ge1$, and $d\ge0$, the numerical range $W(A)$ has constant width $d$ if and only if it is a closed disk of radius $d/2$ (a single point when $d=0$). The proof writes the width in direction $\zeta$ as the gap between the extreme eigenvalues of the Hermitian matrix $H(\zeta)=\frac12(\zeta^{-1}A+\zeta A^*)$, shows by a greatest-common-divisor argument that the midpoint of the projected interval is a rational function of $\zeta$, bounds it by the operator norm to get a Laurent polynomial $a_{-1}\zeta^{-1}+a_0+a_1\zeta$, and uses reversal of direction and reality on the unit circle to identify it with $\mathrm{Re}(\bar\zeta c)$ for one point $c$, the centre. Not addressed: the analogous conjecture of Chien, Li and Nakazato for higher-rank numerical ranges, and operators on infinite-dimensional spaces.
edits.verificationNote: Unreviewed: no independent mathematician is on public record for this proof. No gap was found in that reading, which is this site's own and not an expert review. edits.significanceNote: A conjecture from a 2019 Linear Algebra and its Applications paper, taken up in one follow-up on higher-rank numerical ranges and otherwise little cited; known to the numerical range community only, and settled here in two pages. edits.name: Petty's polar projection problem
edits.field: Convex geometry; projection bodies
edits.statement: For a convex body $K\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ the projection body $\Pi K$ has support function $h_{\Pi K}(u)=\mathrm{vol}_{n-1}(K|u^\perp)$, and its polar $\Pi^*K=(\Pi K)^\circ$ is the polar projection body. For an origin-centred ellipsoid $K$, $\Pi^*K$ is a dilate of $K$. Petty's polar projection problem, which Horvath and Langi call a famous problem of convex geometry and state as a conjecture, asks for the converse: if an origin-symmetric convex body $K\subset\mathbb{R}^n$, $n\ge3$, satisfies $\Pi^*K=\lambda K$ for some $\lambda>0$, must $K$ be an ellipsoid? In the plane the answer is no (Radon curves, for example the regular hexagon). Horvath and Langi (2022) showed the problem is equivalent to their translative constant volume conjecture: a centrally symmetric body for which the volume of the convex hull of two touching translates does not depend on the pair is an ellipsoid.
edits.posedBy: C. M. Petty, Isoperimetric problems, Proc. Conf. Convexity and Combinatorial Geometry, Univ. of Oklahoma (1971)
edits.ageNote: Raised by Petty at the 1971 Oklahoma conference (proceedings 1972); discussed by Gruber and by Lutwak. Martini settled a non-symmetric polytope version. Horvath and Langi posed the equivalent translative constant volume conjecture in 2014 and proved the equivalence in 2022.
edits.aiRole: From the paper: OpenAI's ChatGPT was used to explore proof strategies, develop and check mathematical arguments, and draft and revise the exposition. Hexagon's provenance record names the tool as ChatGPT, GPT 6 Astra, labels the work 'Primarily AI-generated text' with human understanding of 'some parts', and carries the author's statement: the entire derivation was verified and re-derived by the author with no issues found; the author came to the problem while adapting ideas from a manuscript on fixed points of the centre of mass, whose line of reasoning is in the appendix; and 'the final key derivation and ideas were completed by AI'.
edits.resultNote: Theorem 1.1: for $n\ge3$ and a convex body $K\subset\mathbb{R}^n$, with $TK=(\Pi K)^\circ$, the following are equivalent: $K$ is an origin-centred ellipsoid; $TK=aK$ for some $a>0$; $T^2K=bK$ for some $b>0$. No symmetry is assumed, since $TK$ is always origin-symmetric. The proof has three steps: a flux identity $\int h_L^{-1}\,dS_L=\int A_L\,dS_K$ for $L=TK$, where $A_C(u)$ is the volume of the central section $C\cap u^\perp$ (Lemma 2.1); the comparison $\int A_K\,dS_L\le\int A_L\,dS_K$ for symmetric $K$ (Proposition 3.1), whose equality case gives, for every direction, a contractive projection onto a hyperplane along it, so that $K$ is an ellipsoid by a theorem of James; and the remark that $T^2K=bK$ forces equality. Corollary 5.1 deduces the translative constant volume conjecture of Horvath and Langi. Dimension two is excluded, as it must be.

edits.name: Sharp ionization bounds for helium and lithium: the exact values of $N_c(2)$ and $N_c(3)$
edits.shortName: Ionization bounds for He and Li
edits.field: Spectral theory; many-body Schrödinger operators
edits.statement: For $N$ nonrelativistic spin-$1/2$ electrons around an infinitely heavy point nucleus of charge $Z$, let $E_N(Z)$ be the ground energy of the Coulomb Hamiltonian $H_N(Z)$ on the fermionic space, and let $N_c(Z)$ be the largest $N$ with $E_N(Z)<E_{N-1}(Z)$: the maximum number of electrons the nucleus can bind. Lieb (1984) proved $N_c(Z)<2Z+1$. This is sharp for hydrogen but allows up to four electrons for helium and six for lithium, and later general bounds did not lower these two limits. What are the exact values of $N_c(2)$ and $N_c(3)$?
edits.posedBy: Left open by Lieb's bound (Phys. Rev. A 29, 1984); part of the ionization problem as surveyed by Nam (EMS Newsl. 118, 2020)
edits.ageNote: Lieb's 1984 bound allowed four electrons for helium and six for lithium. According to the paper, no later general bound lowered these limits until Shelley and Tartakovsky excluded the helium dianion in November 2026. The year is that of Lieb's bound, not of a formally posed question.
edits.resultNote: Theorem 1.1: $N_c(2)=2$ and $N_c(3)=4$. For $Z=2$, $N\ge3$ and for $Z=3$, $N\ge5$ the ground energy $E_N(Z)$ is not an eigenvalue of $H_N(Z)$, so the counts also hold when binding means existence of a ground state. Helium binds no extra electron in its ground state; lithium binds exactly one, with electron affinity above $0.003064860$ hartree. Nonbinding of the dianions uses a weighted form of Lieb's removal identity with a quadratic weight, reduced to finitely many inequalities verified by computer in interval and exact arithmetic. The computer-assisted statements assume the recorded executions and the stated floating-point conditions (Set-up 2.2). Not shown: any $Z\ge4$, the uniform bound $N_c(Z)\le Z+C$ of the ionization conjecture, or anything about metastable or excited anion states.

edits.name: The number of planar central configurations of four bodies: is it always between 32 and 50?
edits.field: Celestial mechanics; central configurations
edits.statement: Four bodies with masses $m_1,\dots,m_4>0$ in the plane form a central configuration if the gravitational acceleration of each body is proportional to its displacement from the centre of mass; these are the shapes of the relative equilibria of the Newtonian four-body problem. Let $N(m)$ be the number of central configurations up to rotation, translation and scaling, mirror images counted separately. Hampton and Moeckel (2006) proved that $N(m)$ is finite for all positive masses, which settled Smale's sixth problem for four bodies, with $32\le N(m)\le 8472$. Simó's numerical experiments (1978) suggest $32\le N(m)\le 50$, and Figueras, Tucker and Zgliczyński (2024) named the unrestricted four-body count as their next challenge, expecting between 32 and 50. What is $N(m)$ for each mass vector, and is it always between 32 and 50?
edits.posedBy: Simó (1978), numerical study of four-body relative equilibria; proved bounds 32 to 8472 by Hampton and Moeckel (2006)
edits.ageNote: Finiteness for four bodies is due to Hampton and Moeckel (Invent. Math. 2006), with bounds 32 and 8472. Albouy (1995-96) found 50 for four equal masses. Figueras, Tucker and Zgliczynski (2024) counted the restricted problem and expected 32 to 50 for the unrestricted one.
edits.resultNote: Theorems 1 and 2: for all positive masses, $N(m)=12+6+2(c_1+c_2+c_3+c_4)$, where 12 counts the collinear configurations (Moulton), 6 the convex ones, and $c_i(m)\in\{1,2,3,4\}$ the concave ones with body $i$ inside, read off from the position of the mass ratios relative to one surface of critical values. Hence $N(m)$ is even with $32\le N(m)\le 50$, every even value occurs, $N=32$ exactly at Palmore's masses $(1,1,1,m^*)$ with $m^*=(81+64\sqrt3)/249$, and $N(1,1,1,1)=50$. Caveats: the surface has no closed form, so $N$ is decided by certified enclosures only for masses off a closed null set; and the convex count 6, hence the upper bound 50, rests on the author's own unrefereed preprint on convex uniqueness (arXiv:2609.35632), whose formalization is part of the Lean development. This is not a new case of Smale's sixth problem: finiteness for four bodies was already known.

edits.name: Smale's sixth problem for six bodies in the plane: finiteness of central configurations for generic masses
edits.shortName: Smale's sixth problem: six bodies, generic
edits.field: Celestial mechanics; central configurations
edits.statement: A configuration $q=(q_1,\ldots,q_n)$ of $n$ distinct points in the plane, carrying positive masses $m_1,\ldots,m_n$, is a central configuration if there are $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$ and $c\in\mathbb{R}^2$ with $$\lambda m_i(q_i-c)=\sum_{j\neq i}\frac{m_i m_j(q_i-q_j)}{|q_i-q_j|^3},\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.$$ Smale's sixth problem asks whether, for every choice of positive masses, the number of central configurations up to similarity is finite. Hampton and Moeckel (2006) proved it for $n=4$, and Albouy and Kaloshin (2012) for $n=5$ outside a codimension-two set of masses. Is it true for $n=6$?
edits.posedBy: Smale, Mathematical problems for the next century (Math. Intelligencer 20, 1998), Problem 6; earlier Chazy (1918) and Wintner (1941)
edits.ageNote: For six bodies, Chang and Chen (2023-2025) reduced the Albouy-Kaloshin method to 117 diagrams and left 24 unresolved; Aquino-Michaels (2026) reduced the question to 11. Jensen and Leykin's tropical method for generic masses was completed only for up to five bodies.
edits.resultNote: Theorem 1.1: there is a nonzero polynomial $F\in\mathbb{Z}[m_1,\ldots,m_6]$ such that for every positive mass vector with $F(m)\neq 0$ the planar six-body problem has finitely many central configurations up to similarity. $F$ is not computed and its zero set is described only in part: the theorem says nothing when three masses are equal (so not for six equal masses) or when one mass is the sum of two others. Finiteness for all positive masses remains open, as the paper says, so this is a partial result on Smale's sixth problem: the six-body analogue of the generic five-body theorem of Albouy and Kaloshin. The proof follows their method: a curve of complex solutions is excluded through the valuations of the mutual distances at its points at infinity, with linear programs, Gröbner bases and interval arithmetic.
edits.aiRole: The paper's acknowledgement, in full: "Generative AI tools were used to write code, run analyses and draft text; the author directed the work and takes full responsibility for its content." No model or vendor is named. The proof is computer-assisted and formalized in Lean, so the code and analyses are a large part of it; the statement does not say which mathematical ideas, if any, came from a model. Hexagon labels the text a mix of human-written and AI-generated, with human understanding of all parts.

edits.name: Orthogonal bases of symmetric unitary matrices in odd dimensions (mixed-unitary rank of the symmetric Werner-Holevo channel)
edits.field: Quantum channels; matrix analysis
edits.statement: Let $S_n$ be the space of complex symmetric $n\times n$ matrices, of dimension $\binom{n+1}{2}$, with the Hilbert-Schmidt inner product $\langle A,B\rangle=\mathrm{Tr}(AB^*)$. Does $S_n$ always have an orthogonal basis consisting of unitary matrices? Girard, Leung, Levick, Li, Paulsen, Poon and Watrous showed this is equivalent to the symmetric Werner-Holevo channel on $M_n$ having mixed-unitary rank equal to its Choi rank $\binom{n+1}{2}$, proved it for even $n$ and $n=3$, and conjectured it for every $n$. The open cases are odd $n$.

edits.name: Tao's question on the relations of a Lie subalgebra
edits.field: Lie algebras; presentations
edits.statement: Let $\mathfrak g$ be the real Lie algebra generated by $D_i,E_i$ ($i=1,2,3,\dots$) subject to $[D_i,D_j]=[E_i,E_j]=0$ and $[D_i,E_j]=[D_j,E_i]$. Let $\mathfrak h$ be the subalgebra generated by the $[D_i,E_j]$ and the $E_i$. It satisfies $[D_i,E_j]=[D_j,E_i]$, $[E_i,E_j]=0$ and, by the Jacobi identity, $[E_i,[D_j,E_k]]=[E_k,[D_j,E_i]]$. Are these a generating set of relations for $\mathfrak h$, or are there further relations among the $[D_i,E_j]$ and $E_i$? In a comment YCor also asked whether the $[D_i,E_j]$, $i\le j$, freely generate a Lie subalgebra of $\mathfrak g$.

edits.name: Automorphy of elliptic Langlands parameters for split groups over global function fields
edits.field: Langlands correspondence over function fields
edits.statement: Let $F$ be a global function field of characteristic $p$, $G$ a split connected reductive group over $F$ with dual group $\widehat G$, and $\ell\ne p$. V. Lafforgue decomposed the cusp forms on $G$ by semisimple parameters $\sigma:\Gamma_F\to\widehat G(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell)$, through excursion operators; his theorem does not say which parameters occur. Conversely: is every semisimple elliptic parameter (continuous, unramified at almost all places, with $C_{\widehat G}(\mathrm{im}\,\sigma)/Z(\widehat G)$ finite) the parameter of a nonzero cusp form on $G$ over $F$ itself? For $GL_n$ this is L. Lafforgue's theorem. Böckle, Harris, Khare and Thorne proved it for everywhere unramified, Zariski dense parameters only after a finite extension of $F$, and wrote that one expects no extension to be needed.

edits.ageNote: No single source poses it. L. Lafforgue proved the GL_n case in 2002; V. Lafforgue built the automorphic-to-Galois direction for all reductive groups (arXiv 2012, JAMS 2018); Boeckle, Harris, Khare and Thorne (arXiv 2016) proved potential automorphy and wrote that one expects the theorem to hold over the field itself.

The three papers were then reviewed in detail, line by line, by GPT and Claude models, in sessions which had not taken part in writing them, and the errors found in this way were corrected. Boyang Hu organized the work and is responsible for the manuscript." Hexagon labels all three 'Primarily AI-generated text', human understanding 'some parts'.

edits.name: Hernandez's quantum Kazhdan-Lusztig conjecture for quantum loop algebras (types $G_2$ and $F_4$)
edits.field: Representation theory of quantum affine algebras
edits.statement: Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex simple Lie algebra and $q$ not a root of unity. Hernandez's quantum Grothendieck ring $K_t$ of finite-dimensional representations of the quantum loop algebra $U_q(L\mathfrak g)$ has a bar-invariant canonical basis $L_t(m)$ indexed by dominant monomials $m$. Conjecture 7.3 of Hernandez, an analogue of the Kazhdan-Lusztig conjecture: the specialization of $L_t(m)$ at $t=1$ is the $q$-character of the simple module $L(m)$, so that the analogues of Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomials give at $t=1$ the multiplicities of simple modules in standard modules. Before this work it was a theorem in types $A$, $D$, $E$ (Nakajima), $B$ (Fujita, Hernandez, Oh and Oya) and $C$ (Fujita and Qin), and open in types $G_2$ and $F_4$.
edits.posedBy: David Hernandez, Algebraic approach to q,t-characters, Conjecture 7.3 (arXiv 2002; Adv. Math. 187, 2004)
edits.ageNote: Nakajima proved the simply-laced case with quiver varieties. Fujita, Hernandez, Oh and Oya (J. reine angew. Math. 2022) settled type B. Fujita and Qin (arXiv, January 2026) settled type C with freezing operators, wrote that the conjecture was still open in full generality, and explained why their method cannot reach exceptional types. That left G2 and F4.
edits.resultNote: Theorem 1.1: for every simple $\mathfrak g$, every non-root-of-unity $q$ and every dominant monomial $m$ with finite support, $L_t(m)|_{t=1}=\chi_q(L(m))$. The new content is types $G_2$ and $F_4$ (Theorem 20.2); the other types are quoted from Nakajima, Fujita-Hernandez-Oh-Oya and Fujita-Qin. The 76-page argument builds a filtration on each simple module from critical cohomology and the Coulomb-branch realization of Varagnolo and Vasserot, shows that the resulting graded characters $S_t(m)$ lie in $K_t$, are bar-invariant and are unitriangular against the standard basis, and concludes $S_t(m)=L_t(m)$. Appendix A is a finite certificate for the non-thin $F_4$ fundamental coefficients. Caveats: the text is AI-written, the Hexagon record is labelled human understanding: no parts, and the contributor does not claim priority and invites others to check it.

edits.name: Lusztig's Fourier matrix conjecture for noncrystallographic Coxeter groups
edits.field: Representation theory; fusion categories; Hecke categories
edits.statement: For a two-sided Kazhdan-Lusztig cell $c$ of a finite Coxeter group $W$, Lusztig defined an asymptotic Hecke category from Soergel bimodules. Its Drinfeld center is a modular tensor category (Elias and Williamson), and for Weyl groups it is the category of unipotent character sheaves supported on $c$. Lusztig's conjecture: for noncrystallographic $W$ (dihedral groups, $H_3$, $H_4$) the $S$-matrix of this center equals the Fourier matrix attached to $c$ by Lusztig, Malle and Broué-Malle in the 1990s. Rogel and Thiel proved it for dihedral groups and for some cells of $H_3$ and $H_4$; other cells were left with two candidate categorifications, and the middle cell of $H_4$ ($a$-value 6), with Malle's 74 by 74 Fourier matrix, was fully open.
edits.posedBy: George Lusztig, Truncated convolution of character sheaves, Section 10 (Bull. Inst. Math. Acad. Sin. 2015)
edits.ageNote: The Fourier matrices date from 1993-94 (Lusztig; Malle for H4; Broué and Malle). Lusztig's proposal is in a paper posted to arXiv in 2013 and printed in 2015. Rogel and Thiel (arXiv 2023, Represent. Theory 2026) proved the dihedral case and several cells of H3 and H4, and wrote that the middle cell of H4 remained a complete mystery.
edits.resultNote: Theorem 1.2: for every finite irreducible noncrystallographic Coxeter group and every two-sided cell $c$, $S_c=F_c^{\mathrm{mod}}$ under a bijection of simple objects with the Fourier family, for the pivotal structure inherited from Soergel bimodules. New here: a relative Hodge-Riemann argument fixing the pivotal signs, which decides the cells left with two options, and the middle cell of $H_4$: a Morita equivalence of Alvis's rank-24 corner with a crossed product of the Fibonacci Hecke category of type $A_3$, an exact tube-algebra computation of its center (74 simple objects) over $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt5)$, and certified ball arithmetic with a cyclotomic separation bound that makes the match with the CHEVIE matrix exact in all 5476 entries. The Morita step rests on a uniqueness theorem of He and Liu (arXiv 2610.41811, October 2026, unrefereed). No geometric construction of character sheaves is claimed. AI-written; the record is labelled human understanding: no parts.

edits.name: Exact diameter of the symmetric group $S_n$ with LRX generators
edits.field: Cayley graphs, permutation groups, diameter
edits.statement: Let $\Gamma_n$ be the undirected Cayley graph of $S_n$ generated by the cyclic shift $L$, its inverse $R$ and the transposition $X$ of the first two positions: a row of $n$ cards, where one move sends the first card to the end, brings the last card to the front, or swaps the first two. What is the diameter of $\Gamma_n$? The values for $n\le 13$ are OEIS A186783 (2011), where it is conjectured that the diameter is $n(n-1)/2$ for all $n>3$. Before this work Chervov et al. had proved $n(n-1)/2-n/2\le \mathrm{diam}\,\Gamma_n\le n(n-1)/2+3n$, and Antiufeev (arXiv, January 2026) had given a proof of the sharp lower bound $n(n-1)/2$.
edits.posedBy: OEIS A186783 (Tony Bartoletti, 2011); the formula n(n-1)/2 was conjectured there by A. Wesolowski (2013) and P. W. Alexandersson (2020)
edits.ageNote: The sequence was computed up to n = 13 between 2011 and 2018. Chervov et al. (CayleyPy, 2025) used the graph as a pathfinding benchmark, identified the conjectured farthest element and proved bounds within about n of the conjecture. Kuppili and Chitturi (2020) bounded only the cost of sorting the reversed permutation.
edits.resultNote: Theorem 1.1: for every $n\ge4$ the diameter of $\Gamma_n$ is $n(n-1)/2$, attained between the identity and $p^*=(1,0,n-1,n-2,\ldots,2)$. The sharp lower bound had been obtained earlier by Antiufeev and is reproved here independently; the matching upper bound, a word of at most $n(n-1)/2$ letters between any two arrangements, is the new part. The paper's proof reduces the upper bound to a finite set of cases ($n\le 2759$ and finitely many parameters) cleared by a C++17 program printed in Appendix E. The Lean 4 formalization proves both bounds, with its finite certificates checked by the Lean kernel. The Lean theorems do not name or classify the extremal permutations, and uniqueness of the farthest element, also conjectured in OEIS, is not claimed. The authors note that A. Guerrieri independently obtained a proof (in preparation).

We mainly used GPT-6 Astra (with reasoning level from Medium to Ultra) within the agentic system as well as within OpenAI Codex. We also used Opus 5.5 for minor checks and editing". Thank you for submitting the paper of Howe, Huffman, Kohlmeyer and Kruer on Euler's 1747 conjecture. It is published as a Candidate at the Unreviewed tier, significance 22.

What was checked here on 19 November: the eight-page paper was read in full, along with its acknowledgment (the AI disclosure is in the paper and on the Hexagon record). Dietmann and Elsholtz's 2019 note was opened; it confirms that the question is Euler's and that only the case of sufficiently large $n$ was known.

A full sieve up to $64^4$ confirms that every $n\equiv 2\pmod 4$ below $16{,}777{,}216$ is a sum of two admissible integers with the smaller one at most 313, and it reproduces the count 1,344,661 and all twelve entries of the paper's Table 1 exactly. The final constant $21235493/33177600<2/3$ and the constants of Lemma 5.1 were confirmed in exact arithmetic, and Proposition 3.1, the key inequality, held in a brute-force test over 24 values of $m$ up to 4389 and all relevant primes.

What was not verified is the spectral step behind Proposition 3.1 (the Hecke operator on the Hurwitz quotient, Jacquet-Langlands and Deligne's bound). The range $n\ge 64^4$ rests on it, so the tier stays Unreviewed and the status Candidate until someone independent has read it. A formal proof or a number theorist's public confirmation would move it up.

edits.name: Euler's 1747 conjecture on sums of two integers with all prime factors congruent to 1 modulo 4
edits.field: Additive number theory
edits.statement: In a letter to Goldbach of 6 May 1747, Euler proposed that every number of the form $4m+2$ is a sum of two numbers of the form $4x+1$, neither of which has a divisor of the form $4p-1$. In modern terms: can every positive integer $n\equiv 2\pmod 4$ be written as $n=a+b$ with $a,b$ positive integers all of whose prime factors are congruent to $1$ modulo $4$ (the integer $1$ is allowed)? Euler saw this as a possible route to the four squares theorem. Dietmann and Elsholtz (2019) proved it for all sufficiently large $n$; the statement for every $n$ remained open.
edits.posedBy: Leonhard Euler, letter to Christian Goldbach, 6 May 1747
edits.ageNote: R. D. James proved a ternary analogue and, by Brun's sieve, an approximation to the binary case. Lemmermeyer drew attention to Euler's question on mathematical websites, and Dietmann and Elsholtz (Banach Center Publ. 118, 2019) answered it for all sufficiently large n, deducing it from results in the modern literature on four squares.
edits.resultNote: Theorem 1.1: every positive $n\equiv2\pmod4$ is $a+b$ with all prime factors of $a$ and $b$ congruent to $1$ modulo $4$. After dividing out the primes $\equiv1\pmod 4$ from $n/2$, the proof counts representations of $n$ as a sum of four squares and bounds those in which some prime $p\equiv3\pmod4$ divides both coordinates of a pair. The key estimate (Proposition 3.1) comes from a Hecke operator on a quotient of $\mathrm{PGL}_2(\mathbb{F}_p)$ by the Hurwitz units, the Jacquet-Langlands correspondence and Deligne's bound, averaged over the normalizer of a nonsplit torus so that the error term does not grow with $p$. Explicit constants give the theorem for $n\ge 64^4=16{,}777{,}216$; the remaining 4,194,304 values are covered by a finite sieve certificate in which the smaller summand never exceeds 313.
edits.aiRole: From the paper's acknowledgment: "OpenAI Codex generated the mathematical argument, performed the exact calculations, and drafted the manuscript under human direction." The Hexagon provenance statement adds: "Some parts of the contribution have been checked and understood by a human." Hexagon labels the work "Primarily AI-generated text" and "Human understanding: some parts". The model behind Codex is not named.

Checked here on 19 November 2026: the Hexagon paper 2611.00370v1 (8 pages; Will Howe, Grant Huffman, Jensen Kohlmeyer and Liam Kruer, Purdue addresses) read in full, with its AI acknowledgment and the Hexagon provenance record. Dietmann and Elsholtz (Banach Center Publ. 118, 2019) was opened: it attributes the question to Euler's letter and proves it for sufficiently large $n$ only. Euler's letter itself was not opened. The finite range was recomputed here with an independent full sieve: every $n\equiv2\pmod4$ below $64^4$ has a decomposition with smaller summand at most 313, and the count 1,344,661 and all twelve entries of the paper's Table 1 were reproduced exactly. The closing constant $21235493/33177600<2/3$ and the two constants of Lemma 5.1 were confirmed in exact arithmetic. The spectral step behind it (Lemma 3.2: the Hecke identification, Jacquet-Langlands and Deligne) was read but not verified, and the range $n\ge 64^4$ depends on it; hence Unreviewed. What remained was an explicit threshold and a finite check. Thank you for sending this in. We are not listing it, and the reason is scope, not the quality of the work, which is unusually well documented.

What was checked here on 19 November 2026: the Hexagon record hexagon:2611.00357v1 by Scott Duke Kominers (ORCID-linked; provenance label "a mix of human-written and AI-generated text", human understanding of all parts). The AI disclosure is in the paper itself and is substantive: GPT-6 Astra identified a key step that made an earlier GRH-conditional argument unconditional. We read the Lean headline statements (fibonacci_criterion and fibonacci_criterion_matrix, the latter stated with Mathlib's own positive-definite matrices and Nat.fib) and they say what Theorem 1.1 says. A search of the 90 Lean files found no sorry, added axiom, native_decide or unsafe code, and the repository's CI run at commit 499b60d (build, lint, kernel replay, axiom audit) is green.

The catalog records answers to questions that someone stated before the work: a named conjecture, a numbered problem, a question in an open-problems section, a tracked bound. Here the question is posed by the paper itself. Its introduction says "We ask the corresponding question for the Fibonacci numbers", and the AI statement says the problem is the author's own. The question as written on the form (is there a finite set of Fibonacci numbers that suffices?) was already answered in general: the paper cites Kim, Kim and Oh (2005) for the fact that every set of positive integers has a finite criterion set, and Kim, Lee and Oh (2022) for the uniqueness of the minimal one. What the paper adds is the explicit set, and we found no earlier source asking for it.

The way back is simple. If an earlier paper, survey or problem list asks for the criterion set of the Fibonacci numbers (or of a family of sequences that plainly includes them), resubmit with that citation and it will be looked at again; on today's evidence it would go in at the Lean-checked tier.

edits.name: Borcherds' finiteness problem for singular-weight automorphic products and the Gritsenko-Nikulin conjecture on strongly reflective modular forms
edits.field: Automorphic forms on orthogonal groups; Borcherds products
edits.statement: Let $L$ be an even lattice of signature $(n,2)$ with $n\ge3$ and $\Gamma$ a finite-index subgroup of $O^+(L)$. A non-constant holomorphic modular form for $\Gamma$ is reflective if its zeros lie on mirrors of reflections in $\Gamma$, and strongly reflective if all these zeros are simple. The weight of a non-constant form is at least $n/2-1$, the singular weight. Borcherds products (automorphic or modular products) are the forms with infinite product expansions produced by the singular theta lift. Borcherds asked in 1995, as Problem 3 of his list of open problems: are there a finite or infinite number of automorphic forms of singular weight that can be written as modular products? Gritsenko and Nikulin conjectured (Conjecture 2.5.5, stated for their Lie reflective automorphic forms, which have simple zeros on mirrors) that such forms, and the lattices that carry them, are finite in number up to rescaling the lattice. In the form studied here: are there only finitely many strongly reflective modular forms on $O(n,2)$, $n\ge3$, up to conjugation and scalar multiples?
edits.posedBy: Richard Borcherds (Invent. Math. 120, 1995, Section 17, Problem 3); Gritsenko and Nikulin (Conjecture 2.5.5, preprint 1996, published 1998)
edits.ageNote: Borcherds's Problem 3 has a second half, whether such forms exist on O(s+2,2) for s > 24; Wang and Williams settled that in 2023 (arXiv 2301.13367) and showed that singular-weight products are strongly reflective. Gritsenko and Nikulin stated their conjecture for Lie reflective forms; the 2026 paper reformulates it for strongly reflective forms.
edits.model: Generative AI (model not named in the source)
edits.aiRole: From the paper's Disclosure of AI use: the authors developed the initial mathematical framework and the proof ideas themselves, and then used generative AI interactively in mathematical exploration, including literature searches and the development, testing and refinement of parts of the proof. edits.resultNote: Theorem 1.3 of arXiv:2611.16819 (Jialin Li and Haowu Wang, Wuhan University, 16 pages): for each fixed $N\ge1$ there are only finitely many reflective modular forms on $O(n,2)$, $n\ge3$, whose zero mirrors all have multiplicity at most $N$, up to the equivalence $F_2=c\,(F_1|_k\gamma)$ with $c\in\mathbb{C}^\times$ and $\gamma\in O(n,2)$. All weights, multiplier systems, finite-index subgroups and even lattices of signature $(n,2)$ are allowed. With $N=1$ this is finiteness of strongly reflective modular forms and, through Wang-Williams, of holomorphic automorphic products of singular weight. Corollary 1.4: up to conjugation, only finitely many arithmetic groups $\Gamma\subset O^+(n,2)$ have a freely generated algebra of modular forms. The theorem gives finiteness, not a classification, and it is stated with the multiplicity bound $N$: finiteness of all reflective forms at once is not claimed.

edits.name: The coercivity conjecture for nonlocal energies (Imbert-Silvestre)
edits.field: Nonlocal elliptic equations; fractional Sobolev spaces
edits.statement: For a measurable kernel $K\ge0$ on $\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^n$ and $0<s<1$, let $\mathcal{E}_K(u)=\iint|u(x)-u(z)|^2K(x,z)\,dz\,dx$. Assume the symmetry $K(x,z)=K(z,x)$, the upper bound $r^{2s}\int_{B_{2r}(x)\setminus B_r(x)}K(x,z)\,dz\le\Lambda$ and the directional lower bound $r^{2s-2}\inf_{|e|=1}\int_{B_r(x)}\big(e\cdot(z-x)\big)_+^2K(x,z)\,dz\ge\lambda$, for all $r>0$ and almost every $x$. Does it follow that $[u]_{H^s(\mathbb{R}^n)}^2\le C\,\mathcal{E}_K(u)$ for every $u\in H^s(\mathbb{R}^n)$, with $C=C(n,s,\lambda,\Lambda)$? Here $[u]_{H^s}^2=\iint|u(x)-u(z)|^2|x-z|^{-n-2s}\,dz\,dx$. Imbert and Silvestre, working on the Boltzmann equation without cut-off, wrote that they knew no kernel satisfying the directional lower bound without coercivity and that it is natural to conjecture the implication; Chaker and Silvestre restated it as a conjecture in 2020 and proved coercivity under a stronger density assumption.
edits.posedBy: Cyril Imbert and Luis Silvestre (weak Harnack inequality for the Boltzmann equation without cut-off, arXiv 2016, JEMS 2020); restated by Chaker and Silvestre (2020)
edits.ageNote: Imbert and Silvestre state it in a local, kinetic form with a lower-order L2 term; the global symmetric form in the statement is the one the 2026 paper formulates and settles. Biswas (arXiv 2610.06408, October 2026) proved it under an extra annular Lp bound with p > 1 and answered a related open question from the Fernandez-Real and Ros-Oton book negatively.
edits.aiRole: From Section 1.9 (Use of AI): the project began with a counterexample the authors constructed for small $s$ in dimension one, with its extension to higher dimensions following Stein's construction, and with their own heuristic for coercivity under double symmetry. It then developed over several months through discussions among the authors and sustained interaction with ChatGPT versions 5.5, 5.6 and 6. The authors formulated the questions, proposed approaches and assessed the suggestions; the models served as sounding boards and contributed mathematical ideas, technical extensions, refinements of proofs and help with exposition. All arguments kept in the paper were independently checked and rewritten by the authors.
edits.resultNote: Theorem 1.1 of arXiv:2611.16682 (44 pages): for every $n\ge1$ and $s\in(0,1)$ with $n>2s$ there are $\lambda,\Lambda>0$ and a kernel $K$ satisfying all three hypotheses with $\inf_{0\ne u\in C_c^\infty}\mathcal{E}_K(u)/[u]_{H^s}^2=0$. Kernels smooth away from the diagonal admit no uniform constant either, and a function $w\in H^s_{\mathrm{loc}}$ with $0\le w\le1$ and $\mathcal{E}_K(w)=0$ has oscillation 1 on every ball, so the associated equation has bounded discontinuous weak solutions. This covers every $s$ when $n\ge2$, and $s<1/2$ when $n=1$. Theorem 1.15: for $n=1$ and $1/2<s<1$ the conjecture is true. The case $n=1$, $s=1/2$ is covered by neither theorem. Positive results: coercivity holds under an annular cancellation condition (Theorems 1.3 and 1.4), for kernels comparable to variable stable kernels (Theorem 1.8) and for non-cutoff Boltzmann kernels under a nonconcentration assumption (Theorem 1.12).

edits.name: Is any-dimensional nonnegativity of symmetric functions decidable?
edits.shortName: Decidability of positivity of symmetric functions
edits.field: Real algebraic geometry; symmetric functions, sums of squares
edits.statement: A symmetric function $f\in\mathbb{Q}[p_1,p_2,\ldots]$ in the power sums $p_r=\sum_i X_i^r$ truncates to a symmetric polynomial $f^{(n)}$ in $n$ variables for every $n$. Call $f$ any-dimensional nonnegative if $f^{(n)}\ge0$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ for every $n$. For a fixed $n$ this is decidable (Tarski-Seidenberg), and Artin's solution of Hilbert's 17th problem supplies a sum-of-squares multiplier. Is there an algorithm that decides whether a given $f$ with rational coefficients is any-dimensional nonnegative? Equivalently, is nonnegativity of univariate trace polynomials, that is, polynomials in the unnormalized traces $\operatorname{tr}(X^r)$ of one real symmetric matrix of arbitrary size, decidable? Acevedo, Blekherman, Debus and Riener proved undecidability for several groups of variables and left the single-group case open as a natural question; Debus and Schabert repeated it in 2026 and asked in addition for analogs of Hilbert's 17th problem, meaning certificates of nonnegativity that are uniform in the number of variables.
edits.posedBy: Acevedo, Blekherman, Debus and Riener, The wonderful geometry of the Vandermonde map (arXiv 2023, Section 7)
edits.ageNote: Asked in Section 7 of arXiv 2303.09512 (2023; Found. Comput. Math. 2026), repeated in Debus-Schabert arXiv 2606.27551 (Sections 1 and 8) and listed as problem 559 of the AIM Open Applied Problems repository. The paper also cites Levin and Chandrasekaran for the request for any-dimensional Positivstellensatz results; that source was not opened here.
edits.aiRole: From the paper's AI Declaration: initial proofs of both main results (Theorem 2.2 and Theorem 3.1) were found by GPT 6.0 Astra in September 2026. The authors then verified, simplified and strengthened the proofs with further help from Claude Fable 5.1, and wrote the final presentation themselves, using AI for grammar, spelling and readability. The Lean formalization was almost entirely generated by coding agents (mainly Claude, according to the repository README); the authors say that the statements in AnyDim/Paper.lean are the part they compared with the paper.
edits.resultNote: Theorem 2.2 of arXiv:2611.16690 (Sebastian Debus and Robin Schabert, Konstanz, 17 pages): it is undecidable whether a symmetric function with rational coefficients is nonnegative in every number of variables, already for homogeneous even symmetric functions in $\mathbb{Q}[p_2,p_4,\ldots,p_{46}]$. The proof reduces Hilbert's tenth problem in nine unknowns (Jones) through an explicit map $P\mapsto H_P$. Theorem 3.1: an explicit homogeneous octic $F$ is positive definite in every dimension, yet no nonzero power series $Q$ of bounded degree has $Q^{(n)}$ and $(QF)^{(n)}$ sums of squares for all $n$, so Artin's theorem and the Krivine-Stengle Positivstellensatz have no any-dimensional analog. edits.name: Rohrbach's conjecture on thin $h$-bases of finite groups
edits.field: Finite group theory; thin bases and product decompositions
edits.statement: Let $G$ be a finite group and $h\ge2$. A subset $A\subseteq G$ is an $h$-basis if $A^h=G$, that is, every element of $G$ is a product of $h$ elements of $A$. Counting gives $|A|\ge|G|^{1/h}$ for every $h$-basis. Rohrbach asked in 1937 whether this is sharp up to a constant: for every fixed $h$, is there a constant $c_h$, independent of $G$, such that every finite group $G$ has an $h$-basis $A$ with $|A|\le c_h|G|^{1/h}$?
edits.posedBy: Hans Rohrbach, Anwendung eines Satzes der additiven Zahlentheorie auf eine gruppentheoretische Frage, Math. Z. 42 (1937), 538-542
edits.ageNote: Known before, according to the paper's introduction: h=2 for all finite groups (Kozma and Lev, 1992); every h for nilpotent groups (Jia, 1992) and for solvable and alternating groups (Kozma and Lev, 1994). Babai, Gal, Kimmel and Lokam (2003) asked for one absolute constant in such decompositions, the Modified Rohrbach Problem.
edits.resultNote: Theorem 1.2 of arXiv:2611.16938 (Yong Yang, v1 12 November 2026): for every $h$ there is $c_h$ such that every finite group $G$ has $A\subseteq G$ with $A^h=G$ and $|A|\le c_h|G|^{1/h}$; one may take $c_h=1+C(h-1)$. It follows from the stronger Theorem 1.1: there is an absolute constant $C$ such that for all $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_h\ge0$ with sum $1$ there are $A_1,\dots,A_h\subseteq G$ with $G=A_1\cdots A_h$, $|A_1|\le|G|^{\alpha_1}$ and $|A_i|\le C|G|^{\alpha_i}$ for $i\ge2$. The paper presents this as completing the Modified Rohrbach Problem as well. The proof reduces to finite simple groups by the Kozma-Lev extension lemma and treats the groups of Lie type family by family, so it depends on the classification of finite simple groups. The constant is not explicit: $3(3/2)^{120}$ for the exceptional families, enlarged by an unspecified amount for finitely many small groups and the sporadic groups.
edits.aiRole: From the paper's acknowledgements: "OpenAI's ChatGPT was used for mathematical exploration and editorial assistance. The author checked the final arguments and is responsible for the contents of the paper." The paper does not say which parts of the argument came from the model, or which version was used.

Rohrbach's 1937 papers were not opened either; the statement is taken from the paper and agrees with the MathWorld entry on the conjecture, which already cites this preprint. A web search on 19 November found no public confirmation by another mathematician and no earlier proof for all finite groups.

edits.name: The van der Put-Singer conjecture: the inverse problem in difference Galois theory over $C(x)$
edits.field: Difference Galois theory; inverse problem
edits.statement: Let $C$ be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero and $K=C(x)$ with the shift $\sigma(x)=x+1$. Every linear difference system $\sigma Y=AY$ with $A\in\mathrm{GL}_n(K)$ has a Picard-Vessiot (difference Galois) group, a linear algebraic group over $C$. Van der Put and Singer proved that such a group $G$ always has a cyclic component group $G/G^\circ$, and conjectured the converse: does every linear algebraic group $G$ for which $G/G^\circ$ is cyclic occur as a difference Galois group over $C(x)$?
edits.posedBy: Marius van der Put and Michael F. Singer, Galois Theory of Difference Equations, Lecture Notes in Mathematics 1666 (1997), Chapter 3
edits.ageNote: Known before, according to the paper: connected groups and cyclic extensions of tori, by analytic methods over the complex numbers (van der Put and Singer, 1997) and over every algebraically closed field of characteristic zero by specialization (Feng, Trans. AMS 2021). That the component group must be cyclic is Proposition 1.20 of the monograph.
edits.resultNote: Theorem 1.1 of arXiv:2611.11397 (Ruyong Feng, v1 8 November 2026): for every closed subgroup $G\subseteq\mathrm{GL}_n(C)$ with $G/G^\circ$ cyclic there are $A\in G(K)$, a Picard-Vessiot ring $R$ for $\sigma Y=AY$ and a fundamental matrix $Z\in G(R)$ such that $\tau\mapsto Z^{-1}\tau(Z)$ maps $\mathrm{Aut}_\sigma(R/K)$ onto $G(C)$. Moreover $A(x)=h+O(x^{-2})$ at infinity with $h\in G(C)$ semisimple. With the known necessity this gives: $G$ is a difference Galois group over $C(x)$ if and only if $G/G^\circ$ is cyclic. The new ingredients are the construction of such an $A$ with a condition on its finite singularities, and a rigidity theorem for rational difference-invariant lines; the rest uses Propositions 1.21 and 3.3 of the monograph. The $q$-difference analogue is not treated. A footnote records that the second assertion of the monograph's Proposition 3.2(2) is false in general, with counterexamples.
edits.model: ChatGPT 6 with the MechMath Agent Team (MMAT)
edits.modelMaker: OpenAI; MMAT by the Key Laboratory of Mathematics Mechanization, AMSS, CAS
edits.aiRole: From the paper's abstract: "The original results in this paper were entirely generated by ChatGPT 6 and the MechMath Agent Team (MMAT) developed by the Key Laboratory of Mathematics Mechanization, AMSS, CAS. The author reviewed and simplified the initial proofs and verified the correctness of the results." The contributions section adds that the proofs were generated after the author supplied the reference materials; that they contained both new ingredients, the coefficient matrix with $A(x)=h+O(x^{-2})$ and the rigidity theorem, and concluded by descent over a Picard-Vessiot ring; and that the author replaced the descent by a direct use of Proposition 1.21 of the monograph and simplified the proof of Lemma 3.2. The original AI-generated proofs are posted on the author's page.
edits.verificationNote: Read by this site on 19 November 2026 in the TeX source of arXiv:2611.11397v1 (single author, Ruyong Feng, Academy of Mathematics and Systems Science, Chinese Academy of Sciences): the abstract with its AI statement, the introduction, Theorem 1.1, the contributions section, and the rigidity theorem with its supporting lemmas; the construction sections were skimmed. The proof was not refereed here and there is no formal proof. The monograph of van der Put and Singer was not opened: the conjecture (Chapter 3, page 35) is taken from the paper's citation, and it agrees with Conjecture 6.1 in the source of Feng's earlier paper arXiv:1708.07944, which states it as an if and only if and notes that only sufficiency was open. The file of original AI-generated proofs linked from the paper opens (checked, not read). The acknowledgements thank Michael Singer, who co-posed the conjecture, for suggestions; that is not a public confirmation. A web search found no earlier proof and no public expert reaction.
edits.significanceNote: The inverse problem for the shift over C(x), stated as a conjecture in the standard monograph of the subject in 1997 and open for non-connected groups since; the differential analogue was completed by Hartmann in 2005. A specialist question in difference algebra rather than one the wider field tracks. Level with the explicit presentation of the 2-adic absolute Galois group (25), just above Uchida's open homomorphism conjecture (22), below the Bogomolov-Pop conjecture (32) and well below the Margulis-Platonov conjecture (42).

edits.name: The Theta conjecture of Interdonato and Iraci (with the valley Delta conjecture as a special case)
edits.field: Algebraic combinatorics; Macdonald polynomials, Delta conjecture
edits.statement: Let $\nabla$ be the Bergeron-Garsia nabla operator and $\Theta_f$ the Theta operators of D'Adderio, Iraci and Vanden Wyngaerd, acting on symmetric functions over $\mathbb{Q}(q,t)$. Interdonato and Iraci defined a statistic $\operatorname{dinv}$ on parking functions (labelled Dyck paths) with $k$ decorated rises and $\ell$ decorated contractible valleys, and conjectured that for $d\ge1$ and $k,\ell\ge0$ $$\Theta_{e_\ell}\Theta_{e_k}\nabla e_d=\sum_{\pi\in\mathrm{PF}^{*k,\bullet\ell}_{d+k+\ell}}q^{\operatorname{dinv}(\pi)}t^{\operatorname{area}(\pi)}x^\pi.$$ Is it true? The case $\ell=0$ is the rise version of the Delta conjecture of Haglund, Remmel and Wilson, which is a theorem (D'Adderio and Mellit; Blasiak, Haiman, Morse, Pun and Seelinger). The case $k=0$ is the valley version, which was still open. A refinement by touch number replaces $e_d$ by $E_{d,j}$ and restricts the sum to paths with $\operatorname{touch}(\pi)=j$.
edits.posedBy: Giovanni Interdonato and Alessandro Iraci, The Theta conjecture, arXiv:2609.17744 (September 2026)
edits.ageNote: The Theta conjecture itself is from September 2026, but its valley case is the valley version of the Delta conjecture of Haglund, Remmel and Wilson (Trans. AMS 2018), which Interdonato and Iraci still record as open. The q=1 case was proved by D'Adderio, Interdonato, Iraci and Pagaria in 2026.
edits.resultNote: Theorem 1.4 of arXiv:2611.12451 (Bai, Gu, Lin, Qiu and Zhang, v1 9 November 2026) proves the touching refinement: for $d\ge j\ge1$ and $k,\ell\ge0$, $\Theta_{e_\ell}\Theta_{e_k}\nabla E_{d,j}$ is the sum of $q^{\operatorname{dinv}(\pi)}t^{\operatorname{area}(\pi)}x^\pi$ over $\pi\in\mathrm{PF}^{*k,\bullet\ell}_{d+k+\ell}$ with $\operatorname{touch}(\pi)=j$. Summing over $j$ gives the Theta conjecture (Corollary 1.5(1)). Setting $k=0$ gives the valley Delta conjecture (Corollary 1.5(2)) and, through Iraci and Vanden Wyngaerd, the generalized valley Delta conjecture of Qiu and Wilson (Corollary 1.5(3)). The Lean development checks Theorem 1.4 and the Theta conjecture with the Theta operators on the left side; the Delta-operator forms in Corollary 1.5(2) and (3) are not formalized, and the Lean proof follows a different route from the paper's.

The authors studied and checked all of this material, and wrote the paper themselves. We also checked the main identities by computer for small $n$. The authors take full responsibility for the content of the paper." The repository README adds that the Lean proof is the LeanSF library, "developed by Dun Qiu with OpenAI Codex".

Read by this site on 19 November 2026: the TeX source of arXiv:2611.12451v1 (the conjectures, Theorem 1.4, Corollary 1.5, Definition 2.4, the AI section) and the conjecture and dinv definition in Interdonato and Iraci's arXiv:2609.17744, which agree.
